discovery: Metal-halide perovskite semiconductors for efficient solid-state photovoltaics
motivation: Miyasaka first used methylammonium lead halide perovskites as light absorbers in photovoltaic cells (2009). Park and Snaith independently turned them into stable solid-state devices in 2012, and Snaith showed that the perovskite itself carries charge over long distances, which meant planar thin-film cells could work without a mesoporous scaffold. The underlying physics was a surprise. A solution-processed, defect-tolerant semiconductor has weakly bound excitons, sharp absorption edges, long carrier diffusion lengths and high radiative efficiency, which nobody expected from such a crudely deposited material. Within a decade, single-junction cell efficiencies passed 26% and perovskite-silicon tandems passed 33%. Perovskite LEDs and detectors followed. This work created a new class of semiconductor and changed what the whole community of materials physicists can make and understand. Commercial tandem modules are now reaching the market.
